content: The trial results remain highly valuable as they confirm the inferiority and significantly worse safety profile of drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) regimens that rely on injectable medications and quinolones, excluding newer and repurposed drugs. Importantly, the trial demonstrated that better outcomes can be achieved with a 6-month all-oral regimen compared to traditional 9-month or longer injectable-based regimens, thereby supporting the concept of a 6-month all-oral regimen for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB). Descriptive analyses were conducted on the baseline characteristics of participants across all included studies, covering demographics, diagnostic test results, treatment regimens, and treatment outcomes. Comparative analyses were performed both within individual studies and across multiple studies. Within-study comparisons involved pairwise analyses between short-course (6-month) regimens and relevant comparators, as outlined in the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment for drug-resistant TB (2022 update). For example, trials such as TB-PRACTECAL and NExT were included, and primary outcomes from pre-specified analyses were calculated and reported. Between-study comparisons involved pairwise analyses addressing specific PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions by comparing outcomes among cohorts receiving either the intervention or control regimens relevant to the question. Statistical models were employed to present outcomes as unadjusted and adjusted risk ratios. Adjusted risk ratios were calculated using log-binomial generalized linear regression, with confounders adjusted for using inverse probability propensity score weighting. No convergence issues arose with the log-binomial model. When outcome rates were near the boundary, adjusted risk ratios were not calculated, and only unadjusted risk ratios were presented. For outcomes with zero events, unadjusted risk differences were calculated. Confidence intervals for unadjusted risk differences or ratios were determined using the score method. These methods were applied in cases where one arm of a randomized trial was compared to an external population or in subgroup analyses within randomized trials (e.g., by fluoroquinolone resistance status). Covariate selection for propensity score calculations was based on data availability and clinical knowledge, including factors such as age, gender, baseline smear results, HIV status (including antiretroviral treatment status), prior treatment history, body mass index, smoking status, diabetes diagnosis, baseline cavitation, bilateral disease presence, and fluoroquinolone resistance. For adjusted risk ratio calculations, multiple imputation by chained equations using the within propensity score approach was employed to address missing data in potential confounders when the proportion of missing values was less than 45%. Follow-up timing for regimen comparisons combined results from cohorts with varying follow-up times post-treatment initiation. For shorter regimens, post-treatment follow-up was particularly critical to capture relapse rates, as shorter treatments may fail to completely eradicate Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Where possible, follow-up times between comparison groups were matched to ensure equivalent opportunities for death or relapse. Follow-up time was measured from the start of treatment rather than after treatment completion to minimize the effect of differences in total follow-up time. Analyses were limited to 24 months post-treatment initiation for all cohorts, as no analyses included both intervention and comparator cohorts with more than 24 months of follow-up. Evidence from TB treatment trials indicates that a high proportion of recurrences occur within 12 months, or even 6 months, after stopping treatment. Primary analyses optimized the number of participants included in both groups, particularly for shorter (6–9-month) regimens, to allow for relapse detection. Additional sensitivity analyses were conducted, where possible, to evaluate the effect of follow-up time on treatment outcomes. The decision-making process for recommendations considered not only the magnitude of desirable and undesirable effects and the certainty of the evidence but also how affected individuals value the main outcomes, resource implications, cost-effectiveness, equity, feasibility, and acceptability of the intervention. The certainty of evidence and strength of recommendations were assessed using the GRADE system. Evidence quality was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other considerations. High-quality evidence typically comes from randomized controlled trials, while observational studies or programmatic data are often rated as low or very low quality. The higher the evidence quality, the more likely a strong recommendation can be made. The strength of a recommendation is classified as strong or conditional based on the balance of desirable and undesirable effects, values and preferences, resource use, equity considerations, acceptability, and feasibility. Strong recommendations indicate confidence that the desirable effects outweigh the undesirable effects, while conditional recommendations suggest that desirable effects probably outweigh undesirable effects but require more consideration. The WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment (2022 update) were developed following rigorous evidence review and quality assurance procedures. These guidelines will be published on the WHO website for free download and disseminated widely at international and regional conferences. An operational handbook will also be released to support programmatic implementation of the recommendations. National programs will receive support from WHO and technical and funding partners to prepare plans for managing drug-resistant TB, including creating conducive policy environments, promoting universal health coverage, and allocating resources for staff development and community service delivery. Training frontline healthcare staff and students in critical areas such as diagnosis, regimen design, patient support, treatment monitoring, and adverse reaction management is essential. National programs should engage meaningfully with affected populations, communities, the private sector, and other relevant stakeholders in planning and implementing the recommendations. The uptake of these WHO recommendations will be monitored through annual data collection as part of the WHO Global TB Data Monitoring initiative.
